newsitem.title: ITALY: INSTANT VIEW - Italy on Bundesbank gold statement.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Italy on Bundesbank gold statement.

text.p: The following are reactions from analysts on Italy to the German Bundesbank rejection of the Bonn government's plan to revalue its assets and demand an immediate payout of the profits booked from these hidden reserves.
"This will increase the risk of a delay in EMU, and it will not aid Italy's chance of entry into EMU," said Alex Garrard international economist at UBS in London.

"There is considerable uncertainty over the whole project of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), first with the French elections and now the Bundesbank. This uncertainty over EMU can't be helpful to the Italian bond market," he added.
Lorenzo Stanca, Head of Research at Credito Italiano, Milan, told Reuters Financial Television:
"The lira has lost against the deutschemark more than other European currencies and that is not surprising. The perception we have is that...the lira may now regain some ground.

"One thing is certain after all this, that we are going to have days of strong volatility ahead of us. A war has just begun, an open war between the government and the Bundesbank ...and you cannot be so sure at this stage who will be the winner of this war.

"Clearly, the risk of a delay of EMU, which is the serious risk in all of this, would be the real big news which would hit the Italian market (and) other high yielders in Europe. This risk of a delayed EMU is today slightly higher than yesterday."
The EU Commission said it had no comment on the Bundesbank statement.
Stanca said," I don't see the European Commission taking sides at this stage. There's so much at stake - the credibility of the German central bank is being put at stake.
"It is a German issue and must be solved amongst them. It is difficult to think the German government with elections next year wants to hurt the credibility of the central bank."

Lorenzo Codogno, chief economist at Bank of America in Milan, told Reuters: "the situation is stil very uncertain right now, it pretty much depends on the final outcome of the fighting between the government and the Bundesbank.

"The government said they will go ahead and it is legally binding of course with respect to the Bundesbank. Still, I'm a little bit sceptical that they can really do that with elections in a few months, so to rule against the Bundesbank while the Bundesbank is trying to save the value of the currency I think would be very difficult for them.

"So I don't think that they will actually be able to force the situation and if they don't, which seems more likely, or at least they could change the proposal, for example saying they could reduce the debt but not the deficit which seems very feasible - that is the problem right now.

"The overall philosophy of the Maastricht Treaty is that you can not fudge by using your special items such as the gold revaluation. If they are not going to use the revaluation of gold as a means to reduce the deficit to GDP Germany is unlikely to hit the target and if they don't hit the target there is still a question mark about whether they will be able to accept a little bit of flexibility in the interpretation of the criteria, and if not Germany could actually prefer a delay rather than a broad early start.

"The situation's really messy. I would expect a lot of volatility in the market. If I had to bet, I would go short on Italian assets and possibly long on German assets because in the end I think they will not go ahead and so the German area and the mark will strengthen, regardless of the final outcome regarding EMU decisions.
"The immediate effect would be a weakening of the Italian lira and Italian assets versus the deutschemark," he said.
Craig Shute, fixed income analyst at Bear Stearns in London, described the Bundesbank statement as "incredibly damning."

"I think that delay (to EMU) is the option that people will focus on now for a while...I think you've got to ask yourself the question that if the launch of the euro is delayed, will it happen at all?
"A delay might give Italy more chance (of joining EMU in the first wave), but I think it sounds the death knell for the project," he said.

Marco Pianelli of Nomura in London said that if the German government went ahead, "This indicates that there will be a big group at the start (of EMU) and it will be very difficult to exclude other countries which have resorted to creative accounting in order to qualify.
"The test now is if the Buba's stand on this issue has an impact on public opinion. If so it will make approval of the (gold revaluation) plan more difficult.

"The government is risking its reputation on this. It does not appearing to be risking too much. But there will be tensions and if they get out of hand there must be question marks about the whole EMU project.
-- Milan newsroom +392 66129589
